input.question: How much of the "snow" on an analog T.V. is from the cosmic microwave background radiation?
input.ground_truth: > but I have no idea to estimate how many pixels are actually being lit up by CMBR. Zero. And very little of the overall noise is due to CMBR Thermal noise is a much much larger contributor than CMBR (by a factor of between 100 and 1,000) to the 'snowy' picture on analog televisions. In [this](_URL_0_) thread /u/MrDerpleton provides some great information on how the 'snow' pattern becomes rendered.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How much of the "snow" on an analog T.V. is from the cosmic microwave background radiation?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine your old TV screen when there’s nothing on—it looks all fuzzy and snowy, right? That’s called “static.”

Now, think of the whole universe as a big, big blanket that’s full of tiny, tiny invisible waves called “radiation.” One kind of this radiation is called the “cosmic microwave background.” It’s like a very, very old and gentle radio signal that comes from everywhere in space, even from the very beginning of the universe!

But here’s the thing: the snowy static you see on your TV is mostly NOT from the cosmic microwave background. It’s mostly because the TV isn’t picking up any real TV show, so it shows random fuzz. A tiny, tiny bit of that fuzz *could* be from things like signals from space, but the cosmic microwave background is so weak that your TV can’t see it at all. It’s like trying to hear a whisper in a noisy room—you just can’t!

So, almost **none** of the snowy static on your old TV is from the cosmic microwave background. It’s mostly just the TV being confused and not finding a signal.
